newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels want fresh talks before more releases.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels want fresh talks before more releases.

text.p: The international spokesman for Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages in Lima said on Monday there would be no more releases in the deadlocked siege until the Peruvian government resumed negotiations.

The guerrillas insisted President Alberto Fujimori agree to "a political solution" by sending his negotiator Domingo Palermo for talks inside the besieged residence of the Japanese ambassador and allowing rebels to communicate with their jailed comrades, Isaac Velazco told Reuters.
"There will be no more releases so long as the government fails to agree to a political solution," Velazco said in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.
The rebels demanded the release of some 400 imprisoned colleagues from Peruvian jails.

A single face-to-face meeting December 28 between Palermo and Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the rebel leader inside the compound, represented the start of negotiations, according to Velazco. But President Alberto Fujimori "broke" them off with his subsequent statements, he said.

In a speech on Thursday, Fujimori said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas, whom he called "terrorists," were bent on pointless violence that only served to increase poverty in Peru.
The rebels have not freed any hostages since that speech.
"We have made too many gestures. We have released many people without receiving a single response from the government," Velazco said.

The series of hostage releases -- in which the guerrillas freed more than 430 captives -- stopped after seven men were let out on New Year's Day. The wait for more releases has been the longest since the crisis began.

The deadlock has sparked fears that one false move by the government or rebels could trigger a bloody end to the 20-day siege. In Tokyo Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto warned on Monday the standoff at the besieged residence could get out of hand.

"It will be a protracted battle and situations like that make me worried about an unexpected accident," he told reporters. "There have been miscues on the guerrillas' side and also on the Peruvian government's side," he added without elaborating.
The rebels mined and booby-trapped the residence in anticipation of any assault by government forces.
Cerpa was moving constantly around the building, using important hostages such as Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela as a "human shield," according to a local newspaper.
Peruvian intelligence officials were using a satellite to track movements inside the residence, the newspaper, Expreso, reported.

The images showed the guerrillas operating a rotation system allowing five of them to sleep at any one time, for four hours each day, it reported from Washington, without specifying whether the surveillance satellite was American or Japanese.
Diplomatic activity at the site was dead.

There was no sign of the Red Cross' Michel Minnig, the chief mediator in the crisis, or Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a close friend of Fujimori, who have both regularly entered the compond.
Instead a band of traditional Andean witchdoctors carrying skulls and potions went to the site and beseeched spirits to coax the rebels into freeing the captives.

While Japan urged Peru to look for a peaceful solution to the crisis, Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, adamantly rejected ruling out force until all hostages are released and the guerrillas lay down their arms.

The rebels are widely believed to number about 20 but the Red Cross fuelled speculation there could be more because the organisation provided those inside the residence with 110 portions for each meal -- 16 more than thought necessary.
The rebels burst in on a December 17 cocktail party honouring Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday that was attended by more than 500 people.
